templates.name: Hypothetical finding supports or weakens a single claim (causal, comparison, existence, generalization, prediction)
Hypothetical finding discriminates between competing explanations (support or weaken)
Data description: multi-part, interaction, or passage-plus-data claim
Quotation from a literary work illustrates a claim (single trait, two-part, contrast)
Quotation from a person (participant, respondent, historian, critic, article) supports or challenges a claim

Data description: quantified claim (for each, all except one)

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a proposed ecological effect (the key supplies why seeds would succeed where carcasses have cleared the ground)
items.passage: In August 2016, lightning killed a herd of more than 300 wild reindeer on Norway’s Hardangervidda plateau, and most of the carcasses were left to decompose where they fell. Decomposition kills the vegetation immediately surrounding a large carcass, creating a patch of exposed, nutrient-enriched soil. Studying the site, ecologist S. M. J. G. Steyaert and colleagues found that droppings of ravens, crows, and foxes were concentrated near the carcasses and that the birds’ droppings frequently contained viable seeds of crowberry, a tundra shrub that reproduces predominantly through vegetative growth and only rarely through seedlings. The researchers suggest that by feeding at carcasses, scavengers may help crowberry establish new plants from seed.
items.stem: Which finding about crowberry, if true, would most directly support the suggestion made by Steyaert and colleagues?
options: Most crowberry seeds deposited in bird droppings lose their ability to germinate within a few weeks, long before the next growing season begins.
Bird droppings found far from the carcasses contained viable crowberry seeds about as often as bird droppings found close to the carcasses did.
The ravens and crows that feed at the carcasses also consume crowberries at sites several kilometers away, so the seeds they deposit near the carcasses come from many genetically distinct plants.
Crowberry seeds that land among established mosses and dwarf shrubs seldom yield surviving seedlings, whereas seeds that land where competing plants have been eliminated frequently do.
items.explanation: The suggestion is that scavengers “may help crowberry establish new plants from seed,” even though crowberry reproduces “only rarely through seedlings.” The passage notes that decomposition “kills the vegetation immediately surrounding a large carcass, creating a patch of exposed, nutrient-enriched soil,” and that scavengers’ droppings, with their crowberry seeds, are concentrated near the carcasses. If, as choice D says, crowberry seeds seldom succeed among established vegetation but frequently succeed where competing plants have been eliminated, then the patches around the carcasses are exactly where scavengers are leaving seeds, which explains how scavengers could help crowberry establish from seed there.

A.recipe: OPP: undercuts the seeds' chance to establish
A.why_wrong: If the seeds in droppings soon stop being able to germinate, the seeds scavengers leave near carcasses would be unlikely to produce plants, which weakens the suggestion rather than supporting it.

B.recipe: TRAP: a no-difference comparison that cannot decide the claim
B.why_wrong: It compares how often single droppings hold seeds near and far from carcasses; since the passage says the droppings themselves are concentrated near the carcasses, this says nothing about whether the seeds left there can grow into new plants.

C.recipe: TRAP: bears on where the seeds come from, not whether they establish
C.why_wrong: It shows that the seeds arriving at the site come from many plants, but it gives no reason to think those seeds can produce seedlings at the site, which is what the suggestion requires.

sources.what: Steyaert, Frank, Puliti, Badia, Arnberg, Beardsley et al. 2018, Biology Letters 14(8): 20180388, Special delivery: scavengers direct seed dispersal towards ungulate carcasses: lightning killed 323 wild tundra reindeer on the Hardangervidda plateau on 26 August 2016; carcasses left on site; scavenger (bird and fox) faeces concentrated around carcasses; corvid faeces commonly held viable crowberry (Empetrum nigrum) seeds; crowberry has predominantly vegetative reproduction; vegetation around a decomposing carcass dies, leaving nutrient-rich bare cadaver decomposition islands; whether such seeds germinate and establish in the field remains to be tested

items.notes: Band 7. Ecology. The key supplies the unstated premise (crowberry seedlings fail among established vegetation but succeed on cleared ground), which links two facts stated earlier (carcasses clear the ground; scavenger droppings with seeds gather there). A is the OPP; B and C are TRAPs that engage the claim's own variables (seed-bearing droppings, seed sources) but cannot decide establishment. The key avoids the passage's wording (exposed, nutrient-enriched soil). Full text read on PMC (PMC6127118); first author given with initials only, as the paper does. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: D, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: key supplies an unstated premise (seedlings need cleared ground)
the needed fact (carcasses clear the ground) sits two sentences before the claim
two TRAP distractors (no-difference comparison; seed source rather than establishment)
stem names the claimants, 16 words

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a generalization against a rival account (where language isolates occur)
items.passage: A language isolate, such as Basque in northern Spain and southwestern France, is a language that cannot be shown to be related to any other known language. According to one explanation, isolates are the last survivors of once-widespread language families: as speakers of other languages expanded their territory, they claimed the most productive agricultural land, and the older languages persisted only in areas pressed against coastlines or mountain ranges, where few newcomers chose to settle. After testing this explanation against a worldwide dataset of language locations, linguist Matthias Urban concluded instead that the evidence favors the view that isolates are one manifestation of linguistic diversity in general.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Urban’s conclusion?
options: Isolates are, on average, no closer to coastlines or mountain ranges than other languages are, but they are most common in regions where many unrelated language families are spoken.
Many isolates are spoken in rugged highlands or along remote coastlines that border fertile lowlands now occupied by speakers of a single large language family.
Isolates tend to have considerably fewer speakers than languages belonging to large families do, and many of them are now spoken mainly by older adults in their communities.
Several languages long classified as isolates have since been shown to belong to known families once enough of their vocabulary and grammar had been recorded and compared.
items.explanation: Urban rejects the explanation that isolates survived only “in areas pressed against coastlines or mountain ranges” and concludes that the evidence favors the view that isolates are “one manifestation of linguistic diversity in general.” If that is right, isolates should show no special tie to such barriers and should instead turn up where languages of many kinds are found. Choice A reports both: isolates are no closer to coasts or mountains than other languages, and they are most common where many unrelated families are spoken.

B.why_wrong: Isolates confined to highlands and coasts beside a single expanding family are what the survivors-at-the-margins explanation predicts, the view Urban rejects.

C.recipe: OFF: true-sounding property of isolates unrelated to their distribution
C.why_wrong: The number and ages of speakers say nothing about where isolates occur or whether they track linguistic diversity in general.

D.why_wrong: That some supposed isolates turned out to have relatives concerns how languages are classified, not where true isolates are found or why.

sources.what: Matthias Urban 2021, Royal Society Open Science 8(4): 202232, The geography and development of language isolates: a model of isolate genesis by retreat toward major geographical barriers (coastline, mountain areas, land unattractive to expanding groups, Basque as a case) is pitted against the view that isolates are one manifestation of linguistic diversity generally; tested against a worldwide dataset of language locations and distances to barriers; support found for the general-diversity view

items.notes: Band 6 (plan). Linguistics. The key needs two linked steps: no tie to barriers (rules out the rival) and concentration where diversity is high (fits Urban's view). B is the rival's prediction, C and D are off-target properties of isolates. Full text read on PMC (PMC8059667) for the barrier types (coastline, mountains) and the Basque case. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: A, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding discriminates cultural tradition from local food supply (the key holds availability constant)
items.passage: Hunter-gatherer communities surrounding the Baltic Sea were producing pottery by the late sixth millennium BCE, well before agriculture had reached the region. Analyzing chemical residues preserved in 528 of these early vessels, Blandine Courel and colleagues identified distinct regional patterns: containers from the eastern Baltic predominantly held fish and other aquatic resources, those from the southeastern Baltic predominantly held fat from nonruminant animals (mammals, such as pigs, that do not chew cud), and those from the western Baltic held a considerably more varied assortment of foods. Communities may simply have cooked whatever resources were most abundant locally, but Courel and colleagues argue that these regional cuisines were also shaped by cultural traditions.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Courel and colleagues’ argument over the alternative presented in the text?
options: At each site, the foods identified in the pots closely matched the animals whose bones were most plentiful in that site’s refuse, regardless of which part of the region the site occupied.
In every part of the region, the pots were used mainly for preparing food rather than for producing resins, glues, or other materials.
Sites near the boundary between the eastern and southeastern Baltic left similar mixes of fish and animal bones, but each site’s pots held mainly the foods typical of its own area.
Pots made in the region after farming arrived held a broader range of foods, including milk from domesticated animals, than the earlier hunter-gatherer pots did.
items.explanation: The text sets two explanations against each other: communities “may simply have cooked whatever resources were most abundant locally,” or, as Courel and colleagues argue, the cuisines “were also shaped by cultural traditions.” To favor tradition, a finding has to show cooking that differed even where the available foods did not. Choice C does this: neighboring sites with similar mixes of fish and animal bones, and so similar foods at hand, still filled their pots with the foods typical of their own area, which availability alone cannot explain.

A.why_wrong: If pot contents tracked whichever animals were most plentiful at each site, the regional differences would be explained by what was available nearby, the alternative Courel and colleagues reject.

B.why_wrong: That the pots were used mainly for food is true under either explanation, so it cannot show whether what went into them reflected tradition or local supply.

D.why_wrong: Pots from after farming arrived say nothing about why the earlier hunter-gatherer pots differed from one area to another, which is what the argument concerns.

sources.what: Courel, Robson, Lucquin, Dolbunova, Oras, Adamczak et al. 2020, Royal Society Open Science 7(4): 192016, Organic residue analysis shows sub-regional patterns in the use of pottery by Northern European hunter-gatherers: 528 early vessels from the Baltic, mostly late 6th to 5th millennium cal BC; aquatic resources in the Eastern Baltic, non-ruminant animal fats in the Southeastern Baltic, more variable use (including ruminant products) in the Western Baltic; hunter-gatherer pottery adoption not tied to agriculture; sub-regional cuisines attributed to new culinary ideas culturally contextualized and influenced by traditional practices

items.notes: Band 7. Archaeology. Competing explanations (local supply vs cultural tradition). The key brings in a variable the passage never mentions (bone refuse as a measure of what was available) and holds it constant across a sub-regional boundary, so only the tradition view predicts the pattern. A is the rival's prediction; B fits both views; D is the wrong time window. Wording kept to the paper's claim (shaped by tradition), not that availability played no part. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: competing explanations; the key holds the rival's variable constant
key supplies an unstated measure of availability (bone refuse)
TRAP distractors: consistent with both; wrong time window
stem 18 words, names the claimants and the rival

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding from a field experiment discriminates two routes by which fungi reach woodpecker cavities
items.passage: Red-cockaded woodpeckers, native to pine forests of the southeastern United States, excavate their nesting and roosting cavities in living pines. Wood-decaying fungi commonly colonize these cavities, and researchers have long suspected that the fungi assist excavation by softening the wood. The fungi might simply arrive as airborne spores that settle on any exposed wood, but ecologist Michelle A. Jusino and colleagues hypothesized that the woodpeckers themselves transport the fungi to the trees they excavate. To test this, the team drilled cavity-like holes into living pines under sterile conditions, blocking half of the holes so that the woodpeckers could not reach them.
items.stem: Which finding from the experiment, if true, would most directly support Jusino and colleagues’ hypothesis?
options: Many of the fungal species identified in the woodpeckers’ natural cavities were also captured in spore traps positioned in the open air throughout the same pine forests.
By the experiment’s end, holes accessible to the woodpeckers held fungal communities resembling those of natural cavities, whereas blocked holes held distinctly different ones.
Fungi had begun to grow in both the blocked holes and the holes accessible to the woodpeckers within just a few months of the holes being drilled.
The woodpeckers enlarged holes that were already colonized by wood-decaying fungi considerably more quickly than they enlarged holes in which no such fungi had become established.
items.explanation: Jusino and colleagues hypothesized that “the woodpeckers themselves transport the fungi to the trees they excavate,” rather than the fungi arriving “as airborne spores that settle on any exposed wood.” The blocked holes were exposed to airborne spores but not to the birds, so if the holes accessible to the birds came to resemble natural cavities while the blocked holes did not, the difference must come from the birds’ visits. Choice B reports exactly that contrast.

A.recipe: OPP: points toward the airborne route
A.why_wrong: Finding cavity fungi among airborne spores suggests that the fungi could reach the holes without the birds, which favors the alternative rather than the hypothesis.

C.recipe: TRAP: no difference between the conditions
C.why_wrong: If fungi colonized blocked and open holes alike, the birds’ access made no visible difference, so the finding gives no support to the idea that the birds carry the fungi.

D.recipe: OFF: the other side of the relationship
D.why_wrong: It suggests the fungi help the birds, the long-held suspicion the passage mentions, but it says nothing about how the fungi get into the trees.

sources.what: Jusino, Lindner, Banik, Rose, Walters 2016, Proceedings of the Royal Society B 283(1827): 20160106, Experimental evidence of a symbiosis between red-cockaded woodpeckers and fungi: cavity excavator and fungi associations long hypothesized to facilitate excavation, fungi may soften wood; birds carry fungal communities similar to those in their excavations; 26-month experiment with aseptically drilled excavations in live trees, half inaccessible to the birds; accessible excavations had communities like natural cavities, inaccessible ones significantly different

items.notes: Band 6 (plan). Ecology. Two routes (airborne spores vs the birds); the blocked holes are the control that separates them, and the key is the difference of the two conditions measured against natural cavities. A favors the rival, C is a no-difference TRAP, D is the softening benefit (the other half of the symbiosis). The key reports the study's own result, worded as a hypothetical; the spore-trap and enlargement findings in A and D are invented hypotheticals. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: B, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Data description (a total that combines two measures; the key separates the measure that explains a difference from the one that does not)
items.passage: Numerous crops depend on insects such as bees to transfer pollen between flowers, and the economic value of this pollination service can be estimated by comparing the harvest from blossoms accessible to insects with the harvest from blossoms enclosed to exclude them. Using this approach, a team led by ecologist M. P. D. Garratt calculated the insect pollination benefit per hectare for four commercial apple varieties cultivated in the United Kingdom and then, by combining that figure with the area planted with each variety, estimated each variety’s national benefit. Bramley’s national benefit was more than twice that of any other variety, and a student concludes that this difference resulted primarily from the extensive area devoted to Bramley rather than from a greater benefit per hectare.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the student’s conclusion?
options: Bramley was grown on more land than the other three varieties combined, although its benefit per hectare was slightly lower than that of Gala.
Bramley’s benefit per hectare was slightly lower than Gala’s and only modestly higher than Cox’s, but Bramley was grown on about two to two and a half times as much land as either variety.
Gala had the highest benefit per hectare of the four varieties, and Braeburn had both the lowest benefit per hectare and the smallest planted area.
Cox was grown on more land than Gala was, but Gala’s benefit per hectare was greater than Cox’s by about £2,500.

table.title: Area Planted and Insect Pollination Benefit for Four Apple Varieties in the United Kingdom, 2012
columns: Insect pollination benefit per hectare (thousands of pounds)

items.explanation: A variety’s national benefit combines its benefit per hectare with its planted area, so the student’s conclusion needs data showing that Bramley’s per-hectare benefit is not what sets it apart while its area is. Choice B shows both: Bramley’s benefit per hectare (14.5 thousand pounds) was slightly below Gala’s (14.8) and only modestly above Cox’s (12.3), whereas its 3,326 hectares were about twice Cox’s 1,697 and about two and a half times Gala’s 1,312.

A.recipe: INACC: a compound with one false clause
A.why_wrong: The other three varieties together cover 3,518 hectares (1,697 + 1,312 + 509), more than Bramley’s 3,326, so the first part of the statement is false.

C.recipe: IRREL: accurate comparison of the wrong cells
C.why_wrong: Both parts are accurate, but they concern Gala and Braeburn; neither compares Bramley’s area or benefit per hectare with those of the other varieties.

D.recipe: IRREL: accurate comparison of the wrong pair
D.why_wrong: The comparison of Cox and Gala is accurate (14.8 minus 12.3 is 2.5 thousand pounds), but it says nothing about why Bramley’s national benefit is so much larger.

sources.what: Garratt, Breeze, Boreux, Fountain, McKerchar, Webber et al. 2016, PLoS ONE 11(5): e0153889, Apple pollination: demand depends on variety and supply depends on pollinator identity; Table 1 (UK, 2012): area (ha) Cox 1,697, Gala 1,312, Bramley 3,326, Braeburn 509; total insect pollination benefit per ha (thousands of pounds) 12.3, 14.8, 14.5, 8.5; national totals 20,214.7, 19,374.3, 48,120.6, 4,339.7 thousand pounds; benefits from comparing open-pollinated and pollinator-excluded branches

items.notes: Band 7. Agricultural economics. The passage relation (national benefit combines per-hectare benefit with area) must be applied to two columns; the key compares Bramley with the two varieties closest to it per hectare. A is a compound with one false clause that needs a sum (3,518 vs 3,326); C and D are accurate comparisons of the wrong cells in the key's frame. National totals left out of the table (the passage states Bramley's lead) because the paper's Cox total does not equal area times benefit per hectare exactly. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: B, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: passage relation (total from rate and area) applied before the display bears on the claim
INACC compound that needs a sum to falsify
two accurate comparisons of the wrong cells in the key's frame

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates an indirect claim (a speaker uncertain whether he is to blame; translated drama)
items.passage: Drayman Henschel is an 1898 play by Gerhart Hauptmann, translated in 1913 by Ludwig Lewisohn. Henschel, a carter, promised his dying wife that he would not marry their servant, Hanne, but he subsequently married her, and a succession of misfortunes followed. Late in the play, conversing with a friend, Henschel reveals that he remains uncertain whether he himself is responsible for these misfortunes: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from Drayman Henschel most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “A bad man I’ve come to be, only it’s no fault o’ mine. I just, somehow, stumbled into it all. Maybe it’s my fault too. You c’n say so if you want to.”
“No, no; we c’n talk about it a bit. You see, I know ’tis all my fault—I know that, an’ with that we can let it be.”
“I noticed it well enough in my own thoughts that fate was against me. But when my wife went away from me, I had a minute in my own mind when I thought to myself: Now it’s enough.”
“She can’t find no rest in the grave. She comes an’ she goes an’ she finds no rest.—I curry the horses; there she stands.”
items.explanation: The claim is that Henschel “remains uncertain whether he himself is responsible for these misfortunes.” In choice A he first denies responsibility (“it’s no fault o’ mine. I just, somehow, stumbled into it all”) and then takes it back in part (“Maybe it’s my fault too”), so within a few sentences he moves between excusing himself and accepting blame without deciding.

B.recipe: HALF: the same speaker settled on self-blame
B.why_wrong: Here Henschel is certain (“I know ’tis all my fault,” he says, and “I know that”) and wants to close the matter, so the quotation shows a settled acceptance of blame, not uncertainty about it.

C.recipe: HALF: the same speaker blaming fate, in grief
C.why_wrong: Henschel attributes his losses to fate (“fate was against me”) and recalls the despair he felt at his wife’s death, but he never considers that he may be at fault.

D.recipe: OFF: the same speaker haunted, in a nearby state of mind
D.why_wrong: Henschel describes seeing his dead wife everywhere, which shows that he is haunted, but he says nothing here about whether he is to blame.

sources.what: Gerhart Hauptmann, The Dramatic Works, Volume II: Social Dramas, ed. Ludwig Lewisohn (1913), Drayman Henschel (Fuhrmann Henschel, 1898), translated by the editor; the promise to his dying first wife not to marry Hanne in act 1; all four quotations are Henschel's lines in act 5, checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text (double hyphens rendered as closed em dashes, straight quotes as curly)

items.notes: Band 7. Translated drama (premiered 1898; Lewisohn translation 1913). All four options are Henschel in one late scene, in neighboring states: settled self-blame (B), fate and grief (C), haunting (D), and the wavering between excuse and blame (A). The claim is indirect (remains uncertain whether he is responsible). Hauptmann appears in no official item of any skill and nowhere in our bank. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: A, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: indirect claim (uncertain whether he is responsible)
all options the same speaker in nearby states (settled blame, fate and grief, haunting)
older translated dialect language

items.subtype: Quotation from an art historian supports a claim made inside a qualification of a common view (works read as records of time, not single pictures)
items.passage: Aminah Brenda Lynn Robinson (1940–2015) spent most of her life in Columbus, Ohio, where she created what she called RagGonNons: extraordinarily long works assembled from cloth, buttons, and other found materials, then sewn and painted with scenes of Black community life. The name suggests a piece that “rags on and on,” and some required decades to complete; one, depicting Columbus’s Water Street, took 25 years. Because the RagGonNons portray actual streets and residents, they are frequently valued primarily as historical documents. That interpretation is reasonable, a student argues, but it overlooks what the works’ prolonged making reveals: each is less a fixed depiction of a neighborhood than an accumulation of everything Robinson observed there over many years.
items.stem: Which quotation from an art historian would most directly support the student’s argument?
options: “Robinson’s RagGonNons are, first and last, an archive. Buildings since torn down, shops long closed, and neighbors who would otherwise have gone unrecorded survive in them with a precision that makes the works indispensable to anyone reconstructing the history of Columbus’s Black neighborhoods.”

“Into the RagGonNons Robinson stitched buttons, beads, shells, and scraps of cloth, and she painted with a mud-like mixture her father had taught her to make, so that the surfaces themselves carry the textures of the household crafts she learned as a child in Columbus.”

“A RagGonNon was never finished in the ordinary sense. Robinson came back to a piece again and again over the years, so that a single length of cloth holds scenes from many different moments; what it preserves is not one view of a street but the long span of her attention to it.”

“There is no need to choose between treating the RagGonNons as history and treating them as art: their crowded scenes inform us about life in Columbus, while their rhythms of color and pattern reward attention in their own right.”
items.explanation: The student grants that the RagGonNons record local history but argues that, because of their long making, each is “less a fixed depiction of a neighborhood than an accumulation of everything Robinson observed there over many years.” Choice C supports exactly that point: because Robinson returned to a piece for years, one length of cloth “holds scenes from many different moments,” preserving “not one view of a street but the long span of her attention to it.”

A.recipe: OPP: restates the view the student qualifies
A.why_wrong: It praises the RagGonNons as an archive of particular buildings, shops, and neighbors, the documentary reading that the student says is incomplete, and says nothing about how the works’ long making changes what they are.

B.recipe: HALF: the making, but only its materials
B.why_wrong: It describes how the works were made, but only their materials and the crafts behind them; it says nothing about the works being built up over years from what Robinson observed.

D.recipe: TRAP: a reconciliation that misses the claim
D.why_wrong: It reconciles the historical and artistic readings, but neither reading concerns the student’s point that each work accumulates many years of observation rather than showing a single moment.

sources.what: Aminah Brenda Lynn Robinson (1940-2015), Columbus, Ohio artist; RagGonNons, long pieces of fabric filled with diverse materials, the title alluding to their length (the piece rags on and on); some took decades, the Water Street RagGonNon 25 years, showing African Americans' daily life in downtown Columbus; her father taught her a mud-like medium (HawgMawg) she used in her art

items.notes: Band 7. Arts. The claim sits inside the student's qualification of the documentary reading. Quotations are from an unnamed art historian and stay general (no specific canvas details beyond the Wikipedia facts). A argues the view the student calls incomplete; B is the making through materials only; D reconciles history and art without the claim. The key avoids the passage's wording (fixed picture, accumulation). Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: claim inside a qualification of a common view
quotations of about 40 to 52 words that argue
OPP (the documentary view), HALF (making through materials only), TRAP (a reconciliation that misses the claim)

items.subtype: Data description (treatment against two controls; only the procedural control separates the mechanism)
items.passage: Brown bears consume enormous quantities of berries and other fleshy fruits, and many of the seeds they swallow pass through their digestive tracts intact. To determine whether bears are effective dispersers of these plants, Alberto García-Rodríguez, Nuria Selva, and colleagues compared the germination of seeds recovered from bear scats with that of seeds sown inside intact fruits and of seeds whose surrounding pulp had been removed by hand. Because removing the pulp can by itself alter germination, the hand-cleaned seeds allowed the researchers to distinguish the effect of passing through a bear from the effect of losing the pulp. A student who reads the study concludes that seeds that have passed through a bear germinate about as well as hand-cleaned seeds and far better than seeds left in whole fruits, suggesting that bears assist germination mainly by stripping away the pulp.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the student’s conclusion?
options: For each of the four species, seeds recovered from bear scats germinated at a considerably higher rate than seeds sown inside whole fruits did.
Blackthorn seeds recovered from bear scats germinated at a rate of nearly 80 percent, the highest rate shown for any species and treatment.
For each of the four species, seeds cleaned by hand germinated at a higher rate than seeds recovered from bear scats did.
In each species, rates for seeds from bear scats and for hand-cleaned seeds were within 11 percentage points of each other, both well above the rate for seeds in whole fruits.

table.title: Germination of Seeds of Four Plant Species after Three Treatments (%)
columns: Seeds cleaned of pulp by hand

items.explanation: The conclusion has two parts: seeds from bears germinate “about as well as hand-cleaned seeds,” and bears help mainly by removing the pulp, which requires that both treatments beat seeds left in whole fruits. Choice D supports both. In every species, the bear and hand-cleaned rates are close (54.4 and 52.4 for wild rose, 71.8 and 61.2 for alder buckthorn, 22.4 and 30.0 for bilberry, 79.8 and 76.0 for blackthorn), and both are well above the whole-fruit rates (7.6, 37.6, 0.5, and 46.0).

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but against the wrong control
A.why_wrong: Seeds from bears did beat seeds in whole fruits for every species, but that comparison cannot separate the effect of gut passage from the effect of losing the pulp, which is the point of the hand-cleaned seeds.

B.why_wrong: The blackthorn figure is accurate, but one rate for one treatment says nothing about how bear-dispersed seeds compare with hand-cleaned seeds or with seeds in whole fruits.

C.why_wrong: Only bilberry seeds germinated better when cleaned by hand (30.0 against 22.4); for wild rose, alder buckthorn, and blackthorn, seeds from bear scats germinated at higher rates.

sources.what: García-Rodríguez, Albrecht, Szczutkowska, Valido, Farwig, Selva 2021, Scientific Reports 11: 1282, The role of the brown bear Ursus arctos as a legitimate megafaunal seed disperser: germination experiments for 11 fleshy-fruited species (fruits from the Bieszczady Mountains, SE Poland) with three treatments (seeds ingested by bears and recovered from scats, manually depulped, whole fruits); Table 2 germination (%): Rosa sp. 54.4/52.4/7.61, Frangula alnus 71.8/61.2/37.6, Vaccinium myrtillus 22.4/30.0/0.46, Prunus spinosa 79.8/76.0/46.0; ingested seeds germinated at higher percentages than whole fruits and at similar percentages to depulped seeds

items.notes: Band 7. Ecology. Design wrinkle: a third condition (hand-cleaned seeds) that separates gut passage from pulp removal; the key needs both comparisons across every row. A is accurate against the wrong control, B a single cell, C false. Four of the paper's 11 species shown (the four that germinated in the first year with the clearest three-way pattern; species whose whole fruits germinated best, such as Prunus avium and Viburnum, left out, which the conclusion's 'mainly' allows). The pulp-removal inference is attributed to a student; the paper itself reports only that ingested seeds germinated better than whole fruits and similarly to depulped seeds); whole-fruit values rounded (7.61 to 7.6, 0.46 to 0.5). The live Asiatic black bear item concerns uphill seed transport, a different finding. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: D, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: design wrinkle: a procedural third condition (hand-cleaned seeds)
key needs two comparisons in every row
accurate distractor against the wrong control

items.subtype: Data description (a decline in every country plus recovery in some but not all)
items.passage: Measles is so contagious that outbreaks become likely whenever vaccination coverage in a community falls below approximately 95 percent, so public health agencies carefully monitor the proportion of young children who have been immunized. During the COVID-19 pandemic, routine immunization services were disrupted in numerous countries. Examining World Health Organization and UNICEF estimates for five countries, a student asserts that in every one of them, measles vaccination coverage among children aged 12 to 23 months was lower in 2021 than in 2019, and that by 2022 coverage had recovered to at least its 2019 level in some of the five countries while remaining below that level in others.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the student’s assertion?
options: Every country’s 2021 coverage was more than 5 percentage points below its 2019 coverage, and in 2022 only India and Indonesia had coverage at or above their 2019 figures.
Indonesia’s coverage fell from 88% in 2019 to 72% in 2021 and then rose to 92% in 2022, higher than in any other year shown for that country.
In every country, coverage was lower in 2020 than in 2019, and in every country, coverage was higher in 2022 than in 2021.
Coverage was lower in 2021 than in 2019 in every country, and by 2022 every country except the Philippines had returned to at least its 2019 level.

table.title: Measles Vaccination Coverage among Children Aged 12–23 Months in Five Countries, 2019–2022 (%)

items.explanation: The student asserts that coverage was lower in 2021 than in 2019 “in every one of them” and that by 2022 it had recovered to at least its 2019 level in some countries “while remaining below that level in others.” Choice A supports both parts. If every country’s 2021 coverage was more than 5 points below its 2019 coverage, every country was below its 2019 level in 2021 (the drops range from 6 points in India to 19 in the Philippines). And if only India (95% in both years) and Indonesia (92% against 88%) were at or above their 2019 figures in 2022, then recovery occurred in some countries but not in Brazil, Colombia, or the Philippines.

B.why_wrong: The figures for Indonesia are accurate, but one country cannot show that coverage fell in each of the five or that recovery occurred in some countries but not others.

C.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but the wrong pairs of years
C.why_wrong: Both parts are accurate, but neither compares 2021 with 2019 or 2022 with 2019; coverage could rise from 2021 to 2022 in every country without returning to its 2019 level in any of them.

D.recipe: INACC: a compound with one false clause
D.why_wrong: The first part is accurate, but in 2022 Brazil (81% against 91%) and Colombia (88% against 95%), as well as the Philippines, remained below their 2019 levels.

sources.what: World Bank indicator SH.IMM.MEAS, Immunization, measles (% of children ages 12-23 months), source WHO/UNICEF estimates; 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022 values: Brazil 91/79/73/81, Colombia 95/90/86/88, India 95/89/89/95, Indonesia 88/76/72/92, Philippines 83/79/64/76 (API, retrieved 2026-10-27)

items.notes: Band 7. Public health. Two quantified parts (a decline in each country; recovery in some but not all). The key is indirect: the first clause states the universal decline as a bound, the second the partial recovery. C is accurate but uses the adjacent years (a trap for readers who track year-to-year change), D has one false clause, B is one country. The 95 percent threshold is the standard WHO herd-immunity figure for measles (background, not used by the item). Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: A, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: for-each plus some-but-not-all quantifier
indirect key (a bound that implies every decline)
accurate distractor built on the adjacent years

items.subtype: Data description (a balance read through a definition in the passage; alternation rather than a single shift)
items.passage: Mongolia’s exports consist predominantly of coal, copper, and other minerals, whose international prices can fluctuate dramatically from one year to the next. A country records a trade surplus in a given year when the value of its exports exceeds the value of its imports, and a trade deficit when the reverse occurs. Examining World Bank estimates of Mongolia’s exports and imports of goods and services, each expressed as a percentage of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP), an economics student concludes that between 2006 and 2019, Mongolia’s trade balance did not simply shift once from surplus to deficit but instead alternated repeatedly between the two.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the student’s conclusion?
options: Mongolia’s exports were equal to at least 38% of its GDP in every year shown, and they reached about 59% of GDP in 2006, in 2017, and again in 2019.
Imports exceeded exports in 2010 and in 2013, and exports exceeded imports in every year shown after 2013, ending a long period of deficits.
Exports exceeded imports in 2006 and again in 2017, whereas imports exceeded exports in 2010, in 2013, and again in 2019.
The largest gap between imports and exports in any year shown occurred in 2013, when imports exceeded exports by about 22 percentage points of GDP.

table.title: Mongolia’s Exports and Imports of Goods and Services as a Percentage of GDP, Selected Years

items.explanation: By the definition in the text, Mongolia ran a surplus in any year when exports exceeded imports and a deficit when imports exceeded exports. Choice C shows that the balance alternated: a surplus in 2006 (59.4% against 53.5%), deficits in 2010 and 2013, a surplus again in 2017 (59.2% against 56.8%), and a deficit again in 2019 (59.2% against 65.2%). A single shift from surplus to deficit would not produce a return to surplus in 2017 followed by another deficit.

A.recipe: IRREL: levels of one series instead of the balance
A.why_wrong: The export shares are accurate, but exports alone cannot show whether Mongolia ran a surplus or a deficit, which depends on how exports compared with imports in each year.

B.recipe: INACC: misreads the last year as a surplus
B.why_wrong: In 2019 imports (65.2%) exceeded exports (59.2%), so exports did not exceed imports in every year shown after 2013.

D.recipe: IRREL: a single accurate cell comparison
D.why_wrong: The 2013 gap is accurate (61.4 minus 38.9 is about 22 points), but the size of one year’s deficit says nothing about whether the balance moved back and forth.

sources.what: World Bank indicators NE.EXP.GNFS.ZS and NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS, Exports and Imports of goods and services (% of GDP), Mongolia: 2006 59.4/53.5, 2007 59.6/58.3, 2010 46.7/56.7, 2013 38.9/61.4, 2016 50.9/50.2, 2017 59.2/56.8, 2019 59.2/65.2, 2020 57.7/55.2 (API, retrieved 2026-10-27); surplus years 2006, 2007, 2016, 2017, 2020, deficits otherwise 2000-2022

items.notes: Band 7. Economics. The trend matters only through the passage's definition (surplus when exports exceed imports): the student must compare the two columns year by year and see the alternation, as in CB's intermittent-influx item. A gives levels of one series, D a single accurate gap, B a one-time shift with the last year misread. The selected years are representative: in the full 2000-2022 series Mongolia ran surpluses only in 2006-07, 2016-17 and 2020. That minerals dominate Mongolia's exports is background, not used by the item. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.
band7_moves: passage definition (surplus vs deficit) must be applied to two columns
fluctuation rather than a single shift
distractors: levels of one series, a single accurate cell, a misread final year

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim (contentment overshadowed by dread; narrative poem)
items.passage: The Widow in the Bye Street is a 1912 narrative poem by John Masefield. In the poem, Masefield suggests that the title character’s contentment in the life she shares with her grown son is overshadowed by her persistent dread that he will marry and abandon her: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Widow in the Bye Street most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “And room rent ready on the settling day; / And beer for poor old mother, worn and grey, / And fire in frost; and in the widow’s eyes / It seemed the Lord had made earth paradise.”
“Then she would subtly question with her son. / ‘Not very handsome, I don’t think her be?’ / ‘God help the man who marries such an one.’ / Her red eyes peered to spy the mischief done.”
“Her love for him being such she would not rest, / It was a want which ate her out and in, / Another hunger in her withered breast / Pressing her woman’s bones against the skin.”
“One thing alone made life not perfect sweet: / The mother’s daily fear of what would come / When woman and her lovely boy should meet, / When the new wife would break up the old home.”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: the widow is content in her life with her son, and that contentment is “overshadowed by her persistent dread that he will marry and abandon her.” Choice D shows both: “One thing alone made life not perfect sweet” implies that life is otherwise sweet, and the one thing is the mother’s “daily fear” that “the new wife would break up the old home.”

A.why_wrong: It shows the widow’s contentment (“It seemed the Lord had made earth paradise”) but says nothing about any fear of losing her son.

B.recipe: HALF: the dread only, as suspicion of the girls
B.why_wrong: The widow’s sly questions and her watchful “red eyes” suggest her fear that a girl will win her son, but nothing in these lines shows that she is otherwise happy.

C.why_wrong: These lines describe how the widow’s love drove her to go hungry for her son; they show neither her contentment nor any fear that he will leave her for a wife.

sources.what: John Masefield, The Widow in the Bye Street (London: Sidgwick & Jackson, 1912), part I; all four quotations checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text (straight quotes rendered as curly)

items.notes: Medium. Narrative poem, 1912. Two-part claim; A and B each carry one half (HALF), C is a nearby trait of the same character (OFF). All quotations come from the widow stanzas of part I. Masefield appears in no official item of any skill and nowhere in our bank. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: D, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a claim about concealment (a captive feigns loyalty; drama)
items.passage: King Argimenes and the Unknown Warrior is a 1911 play by Lord Dunsany. Argimenes, a king overthrown and enslaved by King Darniak, secretly unearths a sword and prays for assistance in liberating himself. When an overseer accuses him of praying, Argimenes conceals his intentions by pretending to be a devoted servant: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from King Argimenes and the Unknown Warrior most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “Mine arm is stiff with three years’ slavery, and remembers not the sword. But guide thy sword till I have slain six men and armed the strongest slaves, and thou shalt have the sacrifice every year of a hundred goodly oxen.”

“I did but pray to Illuriel to make me a good slave, to teach me to dig well and to pull the rounded stone and to make me not to die when the food is scarce, but to be a good slave to my master the great King.”
“If it had been a hurt!—but we should not complain. I complain more often than you do because I had not learned to submit while I was yet young.”
“No. I have no other hope, for my god was cast down in the temple and broken into three pieces on the day that they surprised us and took me sleeping.”
items.explanation: The claim is that Argimenes “conceals his intentions by pretending to be a devoted servant” when an overseer accuses him of praying. In choice B he admits to praying but claims he asked only “to be a good slave to my master the great King,” a show of loyalty that conceals his real prayer for help in freeing himself.

A.recipe: OPP/LURE: the prayer itself, which reveals his purpose
A.why_wrong: These lines come from the secret prayer to the spirit of the sword’s owner; in them Argimenes openly states his plan to kill guards and arm the slaves, so they show the plans he later hides rather than the hiding of them.

C.recipe: OFF: a frank admission that he has not learned to submit
C.why_wrong: Argimenes candidly admits that he complains because he never learned to submit, which is the opposite of pretending to be a contented, loyal servant.

D.recipe: OFF: hopelessness before he finds the sword
D.why_wrong: Argimenes says he has no hope because his god was broken; he is not deceiving anyone or presenting himself as a loyal servant.

sources.what: Lord Dunsany, Five Plays (1914), King Argimenes and the Unknown Warrior, first act; the book's chronological list dates the play 1911; all four quotations are Argimenes' lines, checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text (double hyphen rendered as a closed em dash)

items.notes: Medium. Drama, 1911. The claim is specific (he pretends to be a devoted servant when accused of praying), so the bare denial No, master is not a fit and is not offered; only B professes devotion to his master. A is the open prayer, C and D are candid speeches to a fellow slave. Dunsany appears in no official item of any skill and nowhere in our bank. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: B, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim about which life stage crosses the sea (comparison of stages)
items.passage: Pachyrhynchus weevils are flightless, yet genetic evidence indicates that these beetles have colonized numerous islands of the western Pacific separated by open ocean. Biologist Hui-Ying Yeh and colleagues hypothesized that the weevils accomplish such crossings not as adults but as larvae transported inside floating fruit. The team therefore exposed weevils at different developmental stages to seawater in the laboratory, and they also placed larvae inside the buoyant fruits of the fish poison tree and released the fruits into the Kuroshio, a current in the Pacific Ocean.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team’s hypothesis?
options: Fruits of the fish poison tree can float in seawater for many weeks without sinking, splitting open, or absorbing enough water to drown anything inside them.
Adult weevils that clung to the outside of floating fruit survived considerably longer in seawater than adult weevils placed in seawater without any fruit did.
Some larvae survived nearly a week adrift inside the fruits and later developed into adults, whereas no adult weevils survived more than two days in seawater.
Larvae that were kept in fresh water in the laboratory survived at considerably higher rates than larvae that were kept in seawater for the same length of time.
items.explanation: The team hypothesized that the weevils cross the ocean “not as adults but as larvae transported inside floating fruit.” Choice C supports both parts of that comparison: larvae survived nearly a week adrift inside the fruits and went on to become adults, while adults could not survive more than two days in seawater.

A.recipe: OFF: the raft, not the weevils
A.why_wrong: That the fruits stay afloat for weeks shows only that the fruit could make the journey; it says nothing about whether larvae, rather than adults, can survive it.

B.why_wrong: It concerns adults riding on fruit, which would point to adults as possible travelers instead of supporting the idea that larvae make the crossings.

D.recipe: IRREL: a true but beside-the-point comparison
D.why_wrong: Comparing larvae in fresh water with larvae in seawater does not show that larvae survive a sea crossing better than adults, or that they can survive one at all.

sources.what: Yeh, Tseng, Lin, Liao, Hsu, Huang et al. 2018, Journal of Experimental Biology 221: jeb190488, Rafting on floating fruit is effective for oceanic dispersal of flightless weevils: genetic data show flightless Pachyrhynchus weevils colonized remote islands; salinity tolerance of eggs, larvae and adults; larvae in fruit of the fish poison tree floated in the Kuroshio Current; no adults survived more than 2 days; after 6 days floating, 2 of 18 larvae survived in the fruit; larvae surviving 7 days of immersion could emerge as adults; eggs and larvae most likely to cross the oceanic barrier

items.notes: Medium. Life science. The claim is a comparison of life stages, so the key needs both the larval survival and the adult failure. A is the raft only, B the wrong stage, D a true comparison that does not bear on the claim (the study did find lower survival in seawater). The key reports the study's own results, simplified (nearly a week for 6 days). Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: C, no second defensible option found.

items.subtype: Data completion (two comparisons of change between two years; near-equal values as traps)
items.passage: In much of eastern Africa, most of the energy that households and businesses consume comes from renewable sources, largely wood and charcoal burned for cooking and heating. As economies have expanded and fuels such as kerosene, gasoline, and liquefied petroleum gas have become more widely available, the renewable share of total energy consumption has generally declined across the region, though by very different amounts from one country to another. For example, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
options: Tanzania’s share fell by about 13 percentage points from 2000 to 2020, whereas Uganda’s share fell by less than 4 points.
Kenya’s share fell by more than Tanzania’s did from 2000 to 2020, even though Kenya’s share was the lowest of the four in both years.
Ethiopia’s share was higher than Uganda’s in 2000, and it was still higher than Uganda’s share in 2020.
Uganda’s share was the highest of the four countries’ shares in 2000, and it remained the highest in 2020.

table.title: Renewable Energy as a Share of Total Final Energy Consumption in Four Countries, 2000 and 2020 (%)

items.explanation: The example must show the renewable share declining by very different amounts in different countries. Tanzania’s share fell from 93.6% to 80.8%, about 13 percentage points, while Uganda’s fell from 95.3% to 91.6%, less than 4 points. Choice A therefore completes the example.

B.recipe: INACC: a compound with one false clause
B.why_wrong: Kenya’s share was the lowest in both years, but it fell by about 8 points (76.8 to 69.0), less than Tanzania’s drop of about 13.

C.recipe: WDIR: a near-equal pair read the wrong way in 2020
C.why_wrong: Ethiopia’s share was slightly higher than Uganda’s in 2000 (95.5 against 95.3), but in 2020 it was lower (90.7 against 91.6).

D.recipe: INACC: wrong extreme in one year
D.why_wrong: In 2000 Ethiopia’s share (95.5%) was slightly higher than Uganda’s (95.3%), so Uganda’s was not the highest in both years; it also says nothing about different amounts of decline.

sources.what: World Bank indicator EG.FEC.RNEW.ZS, Renewable energy consumption (% of total final energy consumption), source IEA, IRENA, UN Statistics Division, World Bank, WHO (Tracking SDG 7); 2000 and 2020 values: Ethiopia 95.5/90.7, Kenya 76.8/69.0, Tanzania 93.6/80.8, Uganda 95.3/91.6 (API, retrieved 2026-10-27)

items.notes: Medium. Energy and development. Two comparisons per option (CB 2.32 style). The key computes two declines; C and D turn on the near-equal Ethiopia and Uganda values; B has one false clause. That traditional biomass (wood, charcoal) dominates renewable energy use in these countries is background, not used by the item. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: A.

items.subtype: Data completion (shape of one series over time among four)
items.passage: Cassava, a starchy root crop that tolerates drought and infertile soils, is a staple food in many tropical countries, where it is eaten boiled, fried, or ground into flour, and it is also processed into industrial starch and animal feed. Between 2000 and 2020, cassava production expanded steadily in some major producing countries, but it followed a less consistent course in others. In Indonesia, for example, production ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
options: rose in every period shown, climbing from about 16 million metric tons in 2000 to more than 24 million metric tons in 2020.
fell in every period shown, declining from about 23 million metric tons in 2000 to about 18 million metric tons in 2020.
rose from less than 1 million metric tons in 2000 to about 14 million metric tons in 2016 and then leveled off.
rose from about 16 million metric tons in 2000 to about 24 million in 2012 but then fell back to about 16 million by 2020.

figure.title: Cassava Production in Four Countries, 2000–2020
figure.description: Four lines at 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016 and 2020; y-axis 0 to 30 in steps of 5. Brazil: about 23.0, 23.9, 26.7, 23.0, 21.0, 18.2. Ghana: about 8.1, 9.7, 11.4, 14.5, 17.8, 24.4. Indonesia: about 16.1, 19.4, 21.6, 24.2, 20.3, 16.3. Cambodia: about 0.1, 0.4, 3.7, 7.6, 14.2, 13.6. Indonesia rises to its peak in 2012 and falls back to its 2000 level by 2020.

items.explanation: The example needs a country whose production followed “a less consistent course,” and it must describe Indonesia. Indonesia’s line rises from about 16 million metric tons in 2000 to about 24 million in 2012 and then falls back to about 16 million in 2020. Choice D therefore completes the example.

A.recipe: INACC: Indonesia read as a steady rise
A.why_wrong: Indonesia’s production fell after 2012 and was only about 16 million metric tons in 2020; a steady rise to more than 24 million describes Ghana, not Indonesia.

B.recipe: WGRP: the values of another country
B.why_wrong: About 23 million falling to about 18 million are Brazil’s endpoints, not Indonesia’s, and even Brazil’s production rose between 2000 and 2008.

C.why_wrong: Production rising from less than 1 million to about 14 million describes Cambodia; Indonesia produced about 16 million metric tons in 2000.

sources.what: FAO (FAOSTAT) data via Our World in Data grapher cassava-production, Fresh cassava production (tonnes): Brazil, Ghana, Indonesia, Cambodia at 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 (rounded to 0.1 million tonnes), retrieved 2026-10-27

items.notes: Medium. Agriculture. Trend shape in one of four series (CB 2.15, 2.34). The key gives Indonesia's rise and fall; A misreads Indonesia, B and C borrow other countries' lines. Values rounded from FAO tonnes. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: D.

items.subtype: Data description (treated vs untreated change from a before measure to an after measure)
items.passage: Common hamsters hibernate through the winter in underground burrows, rousing periodically to eat from food they have stored. Ecologist Carina Siutz and colleagues provided sunflower seeds, an energy-rich food, to some free-ranging hamsters in southern Vienna, Austria, shortly before hibernation began, while other hamsters received no additional food. The researchers weighed the animals when they entered hibernation in autumn and again when they emerged in spring, and they concluded that the supplemental food enabled male hamsters to gain body mass over the winter.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers’ conclusion?
options: When they entered hibernation, supplemented males weighed about 339 grams on average, slightly more than unsupplemented males, who weighed about 334 grams.
Supplemented males weighed about 80 grams more in spring than in autumn, whereas unsupplemented males weighed about 14 grams less.
In spring, supplemented females weighed less on average than unsupplemented females did, by a margin of more than 50 grams per animal.
Both supplemented and unsupplemented males weighed more in spring than in autumn, but the supplemented males gained more mass than the unsupplemented males did.

table.title: Average Body Mass of Common Hamsters at the Start and End of Hibernation (grams)

items.explanation: The conclusion is that the extra food “enabled male hamsters to gain body mass over the winter,” so the data must show supplemented males gaining mass from autumn to spring while males without the food did not. Choice B does: supplemented males went from 339.3 to 419.7 grams, a gain of about 80 grams, while unsupplemented males went from 333.9 to 319.9 grams, a loss of about 14 grams.

A.why_wrong: The autumn weights are accurate, but they were taken before the winter, so they cannot show any change in mass over the winter.

C.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but the wrong group
C.why_wrong: The spring weights of females are accurate (259.5 against 317.2), but the conclusion concerns males.

D.recipe: INACC: misreads the control group's change
D.why_wrong: Unsupplemented males weighed less in spring (319.9 grams) than in autumn (333.9 grams), so they did not gain mass.

sources.what: Siutz, Valent, Ammann, Niebauer, Millesi 2018, Scientific Reports 8: 13286, Sex-specific effects of food supplementation on hibernation performance and reproductive timing in free-ranging common hamsters: free-ranging urban population in southern Vienna; sunflower seeds provided shortly before winter; body mass at immergence: supplemented males 339.3 g, unsupplemented males 333.9 g, supplemented females 294.7 g, unsupplemented females 330.2 g; at emergence: 419.7, 319.9, 259.5, 317.2 g; supplemented males emerged heavier and gained mass over winter, unsupplemented males lost mass

items.notes: Medium. Animal physiology. Treated vs untreated with a before measure (CB 2.25, 2.3): the key is the change in both male groups; A uses the before measure only, C the wrong sex, D misreads the control. Values are the paper's means as given in its text. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: B.

items.subtype: Data completion (lookup in a species-by-year table)
items.passage: Planting designers in Germany have increasingly used North American prairie plants in public green spaces, valuing them as colorful and easy to maintain. To learn which species establish well under central European conditions, landscape researchers Anja Schmithals and Norbert Kühn monitored experimental prairie plantings in Berlin for three years, recording the average percentage of each species’ original plants that survived. Some species persisted almost completely, while others steadily dwindled. According to the table, the average survival rate of narrow-leaved purple coneflower had fallen to ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: 46.5 percent by 2013.
25.0 percent by 2013.
17.6 percent by 2013.
35.4 percent by 2013.

table.title: Average Survival Rates of Four Prairie Species in Experimental Plantings in Berlin (%)

items.explanation: The statement asks for the survival rate of narrow-leaved purple coneflower at the end of the study. In the table, that species’ rate in 2013 is 17.6 percent, so choice C completes the statement.

A.why_wrong: 46.5 percent is the 2012 rate for rough blazing star, not the 2013 rate for narrow-leaved purple coneflower.

B.recipe: WGRP: the right species, the wrong year
B.why_wrong: 25.0 percent is narrow-leaved purple coneflower’s rate in 2012; by 2013 it had fallen to 17.6 percent.

D.recipe: WGRP: the right year, the wrong species
D.why_wrong: 35.4 percent is the 2013 rate for rough blazing star.

sources.what: Schmithals, Kühn 2014, PLoS ONE 9(10): e108588, To burn or not to burn? Effect of management strategy on North American prairie vegetation for public urban areas in Germany: experiment site on Berlin Institute of Technology property, south-western Berlin; Table 2 average survival rates (%) in 2011, 2012, 2013: Schizachyrium scoparium 100.0/99.6/97.8, Liatris aspera 76.4/46.5/35.4, Echinacea angustifolia 50.5/25.0/17.6, Dalea purpurea 61.1/5.5/1.3

items.notes: Medium. Horticulture and ecology. Lookup in a two-way table (CB 2.41): the distractors are the same species in another year, another species in the same year, and another species and year. Common names used for Schizachyrium scoparium, Liatris aspera, Echinacea angustifolia and Dalea purpurea. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: C.

items.subtype: Data completion (one named cell, value-only options)
items.passage: On most railways, locomotives depend on friction between their wheels and the rails, which limits how steeply a line can climb. Rack railways overcome this limitation with a toothed rail laid between the ordinary rails: a cogwheel beneath the train engages the teeth and hauls the train up the mountainside. A student researching mountain rack railways finds that the Snowdon Mountain Railway in Wales, completed in 1896, has a maximum gradient of ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
items.explanation: According to the table, the Snowdon Mountain Railway, completed in 1896, has a maximum gradient of 18%, so choice A completes the statement.

B.why_wrong: 25% is the maximum gradient of the Wengernalp Railway, not the Snowdon Mountain Railway.

C.why_wrong: 37% is the maximum gradient of the Mount Washington Cog Railway.

D.why_wrong: 48% is the maximum gradient of the Pilatus Railway.

sources.what: Wikipedia articles: Snowdon Mountain Railway (opened 6 April 1896; steepest gradient 1 in 5.5, 18.2%); Pilatus Railway (opened 4 June 1889; maximum gradient 48%); Mount Washington Cog Railway (reached the summit July 1869; maximum grade 37%); Wengernalp Railway (opened 1893; maximum incline 25%), retrieved 2026-10-27

items.notes: Easy. Technology and history. One-cell lookup with value-only options, each distractor another row's value (CB 1.38, 1.43). Snowdon's 18.2% rounded to 18. Other rows: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilatus_Railway, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Washington_Cog_Railway, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wengernalp_Railway. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: A.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports an existence claim (some species keep their grip on hot surfaces)
items.passage: In tropical rainforests, the surfaces of sunlit branches high in the canopy can reach temperatures of 55°C. Ants foraging there grip branches using pads on their feet that secrete a liquid adhesive, and because liquids generally become less viscous as temperatures rise, hot branches should cause ants to slip. Biologists Alyssa Y. Stark, Katherine Arstingstall, and Stephen P. Yanoviak systematically measured how firmly workers from 11 canopy ant species clung to surfaces heated to temperatures between 23°C and 55°C. The researchers claim that some of these species maintain their grip as surfaces heat up.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ claim?
options: Most of the ant species tested forage mainly in the early morning, before branches in the canopy reach their highest temperatures.
Workers of several of the species clung to a 55°C surface about as firmly as they clung to a 23°C surface.
Branches in the canopy reach their highest temperatures in the early afternoon, when sunlight is most intense.
Workers of every species tested clung less firmly to a 55°C surface than they did to a 23°C surface.
items.explanation: The researchers claim that “some of these species maintain their grip as surfaces heat up.” Choice B supports this claim directly: workers of several species clung to the hottest surface tested about as firmly as to the coolest one.

A.recipe: OFF: when the ants forage, not how they grip
A.why_wrong: Avoiding the hottest part of the day says nothing about how well the ants grip a hot surface.

C.why_wrong: When branches are hottest is part of the background; it does not show how well any ant species grips a hot surface.

D.why_wrong: If every species gripped less firmly at 55°C, none would maintain its grip as surfaces heat up, which would weaken the claim.

sources.what: Stark, Arstingstall, Yanoviak 2018, Journal of Experimental Biology 221: jeb171843, Adhesive performance of tropical arboreal ants varies with substrate temperature: canopy branch surfaces up to 55 C; ant adhesion depends on liquid secretions that should become less viscous when hot; 580 workers of 11 species tested at 23-55 C; three trends among species, including no relationship with temperature

items.notes: Easy. Life science. One-step operationalization of an existence claim (some species keep their grip). The key matches the study's third trend (no relationship with temperature) in a simple form. A and C are off-target, D is the opposite. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: B.

items.subtype: Quotation from a resident illustrates a single-purpose claim (plants mark burial sites)
items.passage: In BaKongo communities of northern Angola, graves were traditionally left without decorative plants. Yet when botanist Thea Lautenschläger and colleagues surveyed 87 graveyards in Uíge Province between 2015 and 2019, they found plants growing in about three-quarters of them, among the most common being sisal, a kind of agave introduced from the Americas. After reading the study, a student claims that one purpose of these plants is practical: they help people locate burial sites.
items.stem: Which quotation from a resident of Uíge Province would best illustrate the student’s claim?
options: “We plant the same trees that our grandparents planted, because the dead should always be surrounded by the things they knew in life.”
“Many of these plants first came to our villages with the Portuguese long ago, and now we plant them just as they did.”
“In the old days we did not put plants on graves at all; we placed the dead person’s cooking pots and belongings there instead.”
“When the grass grows tall, the graves disappear, but the sisal stays green all year, so we can always find where our people lie.”
items.explanation: The student claims that the plants “help people locate burial sites.” Choice D illustrates this: the resident explains that the graves vanish in tall grass but the evergreen sisal shows “where our people lie.”

A.recipe: OFF: a reason of memory and tradition
A.why_wrong: The resident explains the plants as a link to what the dead knew, not as a way to find the graves.

B.recipe: OFF: where the plants came from
B.why_wrong: It describes the plants’ origin and an outside influence, not any practical use in locating graves.

C.why_wrong: It describes what was placed on graves before plants were used, so it says nothing about what the plants are for.

sources.what: Lautenschläger, Mandombe, Mawunu, Neinhuis 2020, PLoS ONE 15(8): e0236941, Stories told by plants on graveyards in Northern Angola: BaKongo cemeteries traditionally without decorative plants; 87 graveyards in Uíge province documented 2015-2019; 24% without planting; 27 species, most abundant Euphorbia tirucalli (23%) and Agave sisalana (22%); plants used as a marker for graveyards; five interviews with village elders

items.notes: Easy. Ethnobotany. Quotations are invented, from an unnamed resident. The marker use is the study's own finding; the three distractors are off-target (memory, origin, older custom), as in the easy official items. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: D.

items.subtype: Data completion (maximum in one column, with the other column's maximum as a lure)
items.passage: Refractory metals are valued by engineers because they can stand extreme heat: each of the five metals usually placed in this group melts at a temperature above 2,000°C. Their densities, however, vary a great deal, which matters to engineers who design parts for aircraft and spacecraft, where every gram counts. A student comparing the five refractory metals finds that the one with the greatest density is ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: tungsten.
tantalum.
rhenium.
molybdenum.

table.title: Melting Point and Density of Five Refractory Metals

items.explanation: The statement asks for the refractory metal with the greatest density. Rhenium’s density, 21.02 grams per cubic centimeter, is the highest in the table, so choice C completes the statement.

A.recipe: WGRP: the maximum of the other column
A.why_wrong: Tungsten has the highest melting point (3,422°C), but its density, 19.25 grams per cubic centimeter, is lower than rhenium’s.

B.why_wrong: Tantalum’s density, 16.69 grams per cubic centimeter, is lower than those of tungsten and rhenium.

D.why_wrong: Molybdenum’s density, 10.28 grams per cubic centimeter, is among the lowest in the table.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Refractory metals: the five elements niobium, molybdenum, tantalum, tungsten and rhenium are included in all definitions, all melt above 2000 C; property table melting points (C) 2477, 2623, 3017, 3422, 3186 and densities (g/cm3) 8.57, 10.28, 16.69, 19.25, 21.02, retrieved 2026-10-27

items.notes: Easy. Chemistry and engineering. Maximum in one column; tungsten, the maximum of the other column and the best-known of the five, is the lure, so background knowledge does not supply the key. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: C.

items.subtype: Data completion (two comparisons of the same pair, full factorial options)
items.passage: The first electronic computers did their calculations with vacuum tubes, glass devices that switch and strengthen electric current. Each tube used power, gave off heat, and could burn out, so the number of tubes a machine needed strongly affected its reliability. A student researching early computers notes that, compared with the Manchester Baby, the UNIVAC I was completed ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: later and contained more vacuum tubes.
later and contained fewer vacuum tubes.
earlier and contained more vacuum tubes.
earlier and contained fewer vacuum tubes.
items.explanation: According to the table, the Manchester Baby was completed in 1948 with about 550 vacuum tubes, and the UNIVAC I was completed in 1951 with about 6,100. Compared with the Manchester Baby, then, the UNIVAC I was completed later and contained more vacuum tubes, as choice A states.

B.why_wrong: The UNIVAC I was completed later, but it contained about 6,100 tubes, many more than the Manchester Baby’s 550.

C.why_wrong: The UNIVAC I did contain more tubes, but it was completed in 1951, three years after the Manchester Baby.

D.why_wrong: The UNIVAC I was completed later than the Manchester Baby and contained more tubes, not fewer.

sources.what: Wikipedia articles: ENIAC (completed 1945; 18,000 vacuum tubes by the end of its operation); Manchester Baby (first run 21 June 1948; 550 valves); UNIVAC I (first accepted by the Census Bureau 31 March 1951; 6,103 vacuum tubes); IAS machine (operational 10 June 1952; 1,700 vacuum tubes), retrieved 2026-10-27

items.notes: Easy. History of technology. Full 2x2 factorial of two comparisons (CB 1.3). Tube counts rounded (UNIVAC I 6,103 to 6,100); ENIAC's count is the figure Wikipedia gives for the end of its operation, so the column says approximate. Other rows: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ENIAC, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Baby, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAS_machine. Blind solve by the writer, key hidden: A.
